items.title: The determinant lines $\lambda(E)$, $\lambda^*(E)$ and the maps $\lambda(\Phi)$

book.label: §6.2, pp. 203–204
book.statement: $\lambda(E) = \Lambda^{\max}E$ and $\lambda^*(E) = (\lambda(E))^*$. For $\Phi : E \to F$ between spaces of the same dimension, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi(a_n)$, nontrivial iff $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, with $\lambda(\Psi \circ \Phi) = \lambda(\Psi) \circ \lambda(\Phi)$; $\lambda^*(\Phi)$ is the dual of $\lambda(\Phi)$. lean.statement: `maxPow E`, the top exterior power of a finite-dimensional real space, is a line (`finrank_maxPow`), and `maxPowDual E` is its dual. lean.statement: `extOp`: for Fredholm $L$, $\tilde L = L \oplus 0 : E \times \mathbb R \to F$ is Fredholm (`isFredholm_extOp`) with $\ker\tilde L = \ker L \times \mathbb R$ and $\operatorname{coker}\tilde L = \operatorname{coker}L$ (`finrank_ker_extOp`, `extE`, `range_extOp`, `extCoker`). `extDet`: $h \mapsto \tilde h$, $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes d^* \mapsto ((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_n, 0) \wedge e) \otimes d^*$ with $e = (0, 1)$, an isomorphism $\det(L) \cong \det(\tilde L)$ (`extDet_wedge_tmul`); in local determinant charts its coordinate is $(-1)^{\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ times a continuous nowhere-zero function (`coord_extDet`). `extDetN` $= (-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ `extDet` pulls continuous orientations back along $L \mapsto \tilde L$ (`coord_extDetN`, `isLineOrientation_extPull`, `LineOrientation.extPull`) and agrees with `extDet` for $L$ onto (`extDetN_eq_of_surjective`); `extConjOp`, `extConjDet`, `existsUnique_extConjOr`: the same after the swap of the factors. In charts: for $\hat f = \tilde f + S$, $\tilde f(t, y) = f(y)$, $S$ an sc⁺-section of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R \times X$, and the product chart point (`ChartPoint.prodPt`, `ChartPoint.prodT`, `ChartPoint.prodK`), $\hat L(\sigma, v) = Lv$ (`ChartPoint.prodLin`) lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(\hat f, (t, x))$ for every $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ (`ChartPoint.prodLin_mem_linSet`, through the $t$-constant lift `constLift`); an orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ gives exactly one orientation $\hat o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ with $\hat o(\hat L)$ the image of $o(L)$ for **every** $L$ (`ChartPoint.existsUnique_prodOr`, `ChartPoint.prodOr`, `ChartPoint.prodOr_apply`), and $o \mapsto \hat o$ is injective (`ChartPoint.prodOr_injective`).

diff: As we read it, the literal $h \mapsto \tilde h$ is not continuous in $L$ where the parity of $\dim\operatorname{coker}L$ changes, so the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (x, t))$ it defines could depend on the choice of $L$; the sign $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ (the sign of V6.40) is used, which agrees with the text's map when $L$ is onto (Findings, Chapter 6, item 95).

$X \times [0, 1]$ is read as $\mathbb R \times X$ (decision D2), with the parameter first, so $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ is conjugated by the swap of the factors. Only an orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ at the one point and $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x) \ne \emptyset$ (bump functions, V6.1) are used, not an orientation of $f$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 96).
That $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.40, built from an orientation of $f$, is not formalized (gap G.66; Findings, Chapter 6, item 97).

items.title: §6.7.1: the proof of Lemma 6.5

book.label: §6.7.1, pp. 234–235
book.statement: With complements $(V, W)$, a change of the basis of $V$ by $\sigma$ multiplies both wedges of (91) by $\det(\sigma)$, so has no influence. A change of the bases of $A$ and $D$ multiplies $a \otimes d^*$ by $\det(\tau)/\det(\varepsilon)$, and the vector is said to be independent of the bases iff $\det(\tau) = \det(\varepsilon)$. For two choices of complements, the new basis vectors differ from the old by $q_i \in \alpha(A)$ and $p_i \in \beta(C)$, which leaves the wedges unchanged.

lean.statement: `FourTermExact.Choice.exists_smul_source_value`: for two choices of (91) the right-hand sides are related as the sources are. A change of the basis of $Z$ multiplies both wedges by its determinant, a change of the bases of $A$ and $D$ multiplies both sides by the same factor, and a change of complements adds to the basis of $Z$ vectors of $\alpha(A)$ and to the $\gamma$-preimages vectors of $\beta(B)$ (`FourTermExact.Choice.wedgeC`), which leaves the wedges unchanged.

diff: The step "if and only if $\det(\tau) = \det(\varepsilon)$" is read as the homogeneity of (91) in the bases of $A$ and $D$, both sides scaling by $\det(\sigma)/\det(\varepsilon)$, $\tau$ being the $\sigma$ just introduced (possible misprint). The corrections $p_i$ lie in $\beta(B)$ (written $\beta(C)$) and are combinations of the $\beta$-images, whose names are exchanged with those of the $\gamma$-preimages in the last step (possible misprints) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 1).

items.title: §6.7.2: the proof of Proposition 6.12

book.label: §6.7.2, pp. 235–237
book.statement: With $d_i \in R(I - Q)$, bases $a, b$ of $\ker(QT)$ and $a, b, \tilde b$ of $\ker(PT)$, the text computes $\gamma^P_{QT}(\gamma^Q_T(h)) = \alpha^P \otimes (\beta^P)^*$, splits $F/R(P) = \ker\tilde Q \oplus \ker(I - \tilde Q)$, replaces $[QT(\tilde b_i)]$ by $[T(\tilde b_i)]$ in the wedge, and finds the same vector for $\gamma^P_T(h)$.

lean.statement: `mem_span_append_of_ker`: if $Qg = 0$, then $g$ is a combination of the $d_i$ plus $Tx$ with $x \in \ker(QT)$, so the classes of the $d_i$ and $Tb_j$ span what the text calls $\ker\tilde Q$; the classes $[T\tilde b]$ and $[QT\tilde b]$ in $F/R(P)$ differ by elements of that span, which does not change the wedge. With `gammaProj_wedge_tmul` and `comp_comp_eq_of_projLE` this gives Proposition 6.12 (V6.14).

diff: The spanning step is proved directly in $F$; the name $\alpha_q$ in the last part is read as $\alpha^P$ (possible misprint) (Findings, Chapter 6, items 6, 7).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.43: the invariant $\Psi_{(f,o)}$
notFormalized.label: §6.6, Theorem 6.43, p. 231 (proof pp. 231–233)
notFormalized.book: Over a tame $X$ with sc-smooth bump functions, a proper oriented sc-Fredholm section $(f, o)$ defines a linear map $\Psi_{(f,o)} : H^*_{dR}(X, \partial X) \to \mathbb R$ with (1) $\Psi_{(f,o)}([\omega, \tau]) = \int_{S_{f+s}}\omega - \int_{\partial S_{f+s}}\tau$ for every $s$ admissible for $(N, U)$, and (2) $\Psi_{(f_0,o_0)} = \Psi_{(f_1,o_1)}$ for a proper oriented homotopy. For $\partial X = \emptyset$, $\Psi_{(f,o)}([\omega]) = \int_{S_{f+s}}\omega$ on $H^n_{dR}(X)$, $n$ the index (p. 233).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (decision D1). It needs the sc-differential forms and their cohomology of §4.4 (gaps G.37–G.40), integration over oriented compact manifolds with boundary with corners and Stokes' theorem, which Mathlib does not have; its proof also uses the homotopy of Remark 5.16 (gap G.44). What the theorem rests on is formalized: the perturbations of Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) and the tangent orientations of Theorem 6.41 (V6.61) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 100).

notFormalized.title: §6.6: the sections admissible for $(N, U)$
notFormalized.label: §6.6, p. 230
notFormalized.book: For a proper oriented $(f, o)$ over a tame $X$ with bump functions and an auxiliary norm $N$, Theorem 5.18 gives an open $U \supseteq S$ such that every sc⁺-section supported in $U$ with $N(s(x)) \le 1$ has a compact $S_{f+s}$; the distinguished ones, with $(f + s, x)$ in general position at every zero, have oriented solution sets and are called admissible for $(N, U)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as a notion; it is used only in Theorem 6.43 (gap G.54). The facts recalled are formalized: Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) and the tangent orientations of the solution set (V6.61); the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ for a perturbed $f$ is gap G.69 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 101).

notFormalized.title: The facts on paths recalled on p. 201
notFormalized.label: §6.1, before Proposition 6.2, p. 201
notFormalized.book: An M-polyfold is locally path connected, and any two smooth points in the same path component can be joined by an sc⁺-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to X$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond a chart: inside the domain of a chart, nearby smooth points are joined by sc-smooth paths (`exists_nhds_scPath`, V6.49), and "in the same path component" (Definitions 6.27, 6.38) is read as "joined by an sc-smooth path" (V6.58) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 42).

notFormalized.title: The alternative determinant $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$
notFormalized.label: §6.3, after Definition 6.7, p. 208
notFormalized.book: Some authors use $\det(T) = \lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$; the two definitions are naturally isomorphic, given a convention identifying $\lambda^*(A)$ and $\lambda(A^*)$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**, and not used: the chapter's formal statements use Definition 6.7 (V6.8); the convention $\iota$ of Definition 6.3 is V6.3 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 10).

notFormalized.title: The identification (95) and the maps $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$
notFormalized.label: §6.3, after Proposition 6.15, p. 213
notFormalized.book: Dual to (94), $\mathbb R \to \lambda(\mathbb R^n)$ maps $1$ to the wedge of the standard basis, with inverse (95) $c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n \mapsto \det([c_1, \dots, c_n])$; this gives identifications $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ and $V \otimes \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ for every finite-dimensional $V$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**, and not used: the formal statements use (94) only (V6.17, V6.18) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 10).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 6.19 in general
notFormalized.label: §6.4, Lemma 6.19, p. 216
notFormalized.book: For finite-dimensional topological vector bundles $E$, $F$ over $X$, the bundles $\lambda(E)$, $\lambda^*(F)$, $E \oplus F$ and $E \otimes F$ have the structure of topological vector bundles in a natural way (a standard lemma, cited from [29]).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** in general: Mathlib has no exterior powers or tensor products of vector bundles. The lemma is applied only to trivial bundles, and Proposition 6.20 is proved with explicit frames (V6.22) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 22).

notFormalized.title: $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable; the classical case
notFormalized.label: §6.4, p. 218; the opening of §6.5, p. 219
notFormalized.book: The text remarks that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is known to be non-orientable, though orientable over certain subsets. For a classical Fredholm map $f : U \to F$, the determinant line bundle of the $Df(x)$ is a smooth line bundle over $U$, with precisely two orientations if $U$ is contractible.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** (remarks, not used). The orientability over convex sets of Fredholm operators, which is what the chapter uses, is Proposition 6.26 (V6.30) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 26).

notFormalized.title: Proposition 6.28 (1): sc-smooth contractibility
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Proposition 6.28 (1), p. 220; Theorem 6.35, Definition 6.36, Theorem 6.37
notFormalized.book: The neighbourhood $U(x)$ of Proposition 6.28 is sc-smoothly contractible (by $r(ty)$ on $U = r(V')$, $V'$ convex), and Theorem 6.35, Definition 6.36 and property (∗) of Theorem 6.37 ask for sc-smoothly contractible neighbourhoods.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** As we read it, the proof does not establish (1) for $U$: it needs $r(V') \subseteq V'$, which is not stated. (1′) is proved instead (two sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points are sc-smoothly homotopic in a larger $W$ with the end points fixed) and is what the proofs use (V6.32, V6.48, V6.50, V6.57) (Findings, Chapter 6, items 45, 53, 54, 72).

notFormalized.title: Lemma 6.30 as a statement about manifolds
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Lemma 6.30, p. 222
notFormalized.book: The solution set of $F = 0$ near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ is a smooth manifold with boundary with corners, $\pi : S \to [0, 1]$ is a submersion, its fibres $S_t$ are manifolds with boundary with corners, and $L$ is a smooth vector bundle over $[0, 1]$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The kernels are formalized as a continuous family of subspaces of the model space (V6.34, V6.42), which is all the continuation of orientations needs (Findings, Chapter 6, item 48).

notFormalized.title: Property (P) of Lemma 6.29 for the slices $F_t$
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Lemma 6.29, p. 222
notFormalized.book: (P): for every fixed $t \in [0, 1]$, the section $F_t$ is at $(\varphi(t), 0)$ in general position to the boundary of $X \times \mathbb R^k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The general position of $F$ at the points $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, which the text derives from (P) and which Lemmas 6.30, 6.31 use, is proved (V6.33). As we read it, (P) follows, since the tangent vectors of the family of zeros lie in $\ker F'$ and $\mathbb R^n$ has no boundary; this chart computation is not carried out (Findings, Chapter 6, item 47).

notFormalized.title: $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ as sc-Fredholm operators on every level
notFormalized.label: §6.1, Definition 6.1, p. 201
notFormalized.book: The operators in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are sc-Fredholm operators $T_xX \to Y_x$, all with the same Fredholm index.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** on every level: at a chart point the members are shown Fredholm on level $0$, with the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of V3.98, which is what the determinant lines use (V6.1) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 40).

notFormalized.title: Paths and families on $[0, 1]$; $X \times [0, 1]$ as an M-polyfold
notFormalized.label: §6.5, pp. 220–230
notFormalized.book: Paths, homotopies and families are sc-smooth maps on $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$, and $X \times [0, 1]$, $[0, 1] \times X \times \mathbb R^k$ are M-polyfolds with boundary (Proposition 6.28, Lemmas 6.29–6.34, Theorem 6.35, Remark 6.42).
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as stated: they are read on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^n \times X$, of which only $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$ matters (decision D2), as for Proposition 6.2 in Chapter 3 (V3.98); a path that does not extend sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is not covered (Findings, Chapter 6, items 71, 102).

notFormalized.title: Remark 6.42 beyond a point
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Remark 6.42, p. 230
notFormalized.book: $\hat f(x, t) = f(x) + s(x, t)$ on $X \times [0, 1]$ has a natural orientation associated with $o$ and the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** beyond a point: that $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.40 (continuity over the orientable neighbourhoods of $\mathbb R \times X$, independence of the chart of the pull-back bundle), built from an orientation of $f$. At a point the remark is V6.62 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 97).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.41: the orientation of $S$ as a manifold
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.41, p. 229
notFormalized.book: The solution set $S$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners possessing a natural orientation.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized** as an orientation of the abstract finite-dimensional manifold $S$ (of its tangent bundle in the charts of the induced structure). What is formalized is the tangent orientation at each zero and its continuity along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart (V6.61) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 92).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 6.41: tangent orientations read in two charts
notFormalized.label: §6.5, Theorem 6.41, p. 229
notFormalized.book: $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ is oriented by $o^f_x$, an object the text treats as independent of the chart.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: the compatibility of the tangent orientations read in two charts at the same zero. $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ itself is identified between charts (V6.53–V6.55) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 92).

notFormalized.title: The paragraph after Theorem 6.41: perturbed solution sets
notFormalized.label: §6.5, after Theorem 6.41, pp. 229–230
notFormalized.book: If $f$ is not generic, a small perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set gives $S_{f+s}$ a natural orientation coming from $o^f$, since $\det((f + s)'(x))$ is oriented from $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ for $x \in S_{f+s}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**: the perturbation, the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ coming from $o^f$, and the identification $\mathrm{Lin}(f + s, x) = \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ that it uses. The perturbations themselves are Theorem 5.18 (V5.38, V5.39) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 93).
